mainTopic: Feeding the dangerously ill (fixing טבל on שבת), the treatment of בולמוס with stories of the חכמים, and the signs and cause of a כלב שוטה.
overview: This amud finishes the discussion of feeding a dangerously ill person forbidden food. If the טבל can be fixed into חולין, we tithe it, even on שבת and even when the produce grew in an עציץ שאינו נקוב. The גמרא explains that the dispute between בן תימא and the תנא קמא is about whether טבל or תרומה is more severe. It then shows that רבה's rule fits even רבי's lenient view about the snake-bitten person, because grain looks like Torah-level טבל. Next comes בולמוס, a dangerous attack of hunger. It is treated with honey and sweets, but according to אביי only after real food, and several אמוראים list other remedies. Stories follow about רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי suffering בולמוס, and about רבי מאיר, who suspected the innkeeper כידור because of his name and so saved his money. That story ends with the lesson of מים אחרונים, and with the other חכמים also learning to pay attention to names. Finally, the גמרא returns to the משנה's כלב שוטה. It lists the signs of a mad dog and the dispute between רב and שמואל about what causes the madness. The practical difference between their views is given on the next amud.

steps.title: Why say the obvious about using permitted food?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבה's ruling that if one can fix the food into חולין one should, and asks why that needs saying.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is possible to feed him permitted (tithed) food, we should. Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבה's rule: if you can tithe the טבל and turn it into permitted food, do that. Then it asks why רבה needed to say something so obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating טבל is a serious Torah prohibition, so tithing first is clearly better. A rule that seems this obvious must be teaching something hidden. The גמרא now has to find the case where it is a real חידוש.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious! (a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new)

phrases.english: "If it is possible with non-sacred food" — that is obvious!
phrases.notes: He's quoting רבה's rule: tithe the טבל so it becomes permitted חולין.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's statement from the earlier part of the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that one should tithe and feed חולין when possible.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Avoiding a Torah prohibition when it is easy to do is self-evident, so the ruling seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The ruling is needed for שבת
steps.stepSummary: The ruling teaches that one should tithe even on שבת, when tithing is normally forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבה is talking about שבת. On שבת we normally may not separate תרומות ומעשרות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חידוש is that tithing is required even though it breaks a שבת rule. It is still better than feeding the sick person טבל.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (introduces the special case where a rule is a real חידוש)
שבת, when separating tithes is normally forbidden

phrases.english: No, it is necessary for a case on Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge by placing the case on שבת.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא in time: שבת).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought that tithing on שבת is forbidden, so we should just feed him the טבל.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even on שבת, we tithe first rather than feed טבל.

steps.title: Even on שבת it is obvious
steps.stepSummary: The problem with tithing on שבת is only דרבנן. Eating טבל is דאורייתא, so tithing is still obviously better.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even on שבת it is obvious, since the problem of handling is only a rabbinic law!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: even on שבת the answer is obvious. The issue with tithing on שבת (handling the produce, טלטול) is only מדרבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We weigh a rabbinic prohibition (טלטול on שבת) against a Torah prohibition (eating טבל). Of course we pick the lighter, rabbinic one. So the שבת answer still does not explain why רבה needed to say this.

keyTerms.meaning: Moving or handling an object on שבת (here, the produce being tithed)
By rabbinic law, not Torah law

phrases.english: On Shabbat as well, it is obvious —
moving is only a rabbinic prohibition!
phrases.notes: Compare that with eating טבל, which is a Torah prohibition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 2 as still obvious.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that רבה's ruling is a חידוש for שבת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rabbinic prohibition obviously gives way to avoid a Torah prohibition, so there is still no חידוש.

steps.title: A pot without a hole: both sides are rabbinic
steps.stepSummary: The case is produce grown in an עציץ שאינו נקוב. That produce is טבל only מדרבנן, so both sides are equally rabbinic.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A pot with no hole, where the obligation is rabbinic.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the case further. The produce grew in a pot with no hole in the bottom. Such produce is only טבל מדרבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now both options are rabbinic: eating rabbinic טבל, or handling the produce on שבת to tithe it. The חידוש is that even here we still tithe first rather than feed him טבל. Both sides of the dispute agree on this whenever fixing is possible. The dispute about טבל versus תרומה in the next step applies only when fixing is not possible.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing here? (introduces a narrowed case)
A plant pot with no hole, not connected to the ground. Produce grown in it is obligated in tithes only מדרבנן.

steps.confusionAlert: The word דְּרַבָּנַן at the end refers to the טבל status of the produce, not to the שבת rule. The point is that now both sides of the scale are rabbinic.

phrases.english: Here, with what are we dealing?
With an imperforate pot, whose obligation is rabbinic.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 3 by narrowing the case so that both prohibitions are rabbinic.
steps.terutzResolutionType: אוקימתא: limiting the case to an עציץ שאינו נקוב.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: When both sides are only rabbinic, we might think we should not break שבת rules and should simply feed him the rabbinic טבל.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even when the טבל is only rabbinic, one tithes on שבת rather than feed טבל.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה's rule is a real חידוש only for rabbinic טבל (an עציץ שאינו נקוב) on שבת. Even there, we tithe first.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that טבל, even rabbinic טבל, is weighed as heavier than the rabbinic שבת restriction on handling it.

steps.title: The root of the dispute: which is more severe, טבל or תרומה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the earlier dispute. One side holds טבל is more severe; the other holds תרומה is more severe.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage holds טבל is more severe, and one Sage holds תרומה is more severe.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the dispute about whether a sick person should be fed טבל or תרומה. It explains the reasoning behind each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בן תימא says to feed תרומה, because he holds טבל is more severe. The תנא קמא says to feed טבל, because he holds תרומה is more severe. Each side feeds the patient whichever food it considers lighter.

keyTerms.meaning: One Sage holds... and the other Sage holds (lays out the reasoning of two opinions)
Produce from which תרומות ומעשרות have not yet been taken
The portion given to a כהן, forbidden to a non-כהן

steps.confusionAlert: The side that holds טבל is more severe is the one that feeds תרומה (בן תימא), not the one that feeds טבל. Each side feeds the lighter food.

phrases.english: One Sage holds untithed produce is more severe,
phrases.notes: בן תימא, who says to feed תרומה.

phrases.english: and one Sage holds teruma is more severe.
phrases.notes: The תנא קמא, who says to feed טבל.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר סָבַר טֶבֶל חָמוּר, וּמַר סָבַר תְּרוּמָה חֲמוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having settled רבה's case where fixing is possible (which everyone agrees on), returns to explain the base dispute that applies when fixing into חולין is not possible.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dispute over feeding טבל or תרומה depends on which prohibition is considered more severe.

steps.title: Proposal: is this a dispute between תנאים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רבה's rule of tithing first may match one side of an earlier dispute between תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this is a dispute between תנאים?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא proposes that רבה's view is already a dispute between תנאים, and is about to bring a ברייתא to show it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לימא means 'shall we say', a suggestion that will be tested. If it holds, רבה's ruling would agree with only one תנא, and the other תנא would disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a dispute among תנאים

phrases.english: Let us say it is a dispute of tannaim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new line asking whether רבה's ruling is the subject of a tannaitic dispute.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבה's requirement to tithe first is already disputed by תנאים.

steps.title: The snake-bite case: רבי says no need to tithe
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: for someone bitten by a snake on שבת, we do whatever is needed to heal him. רבי says we feed him without tithing.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: someone bitten by a snake — we call a doctor for him from place to place, tear apart a chicken for him, cut leeks for him and feed him, and there is no need to tithe. These are the words of רבי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a person in danger from a snakebite on שבת. רבי rules that we feed him the leeks without tithing them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saving a life overrides שבת, so all these actions are allowed. רבי adds that there is no need to tithe the leeks first. That seems to oppose רבה, who requires tithing when possible.

phrases.english: As it was taught: one whom a snake bit —
one calls a doctor for him from place to place,
phrases.notes: Even if the doctor must travel beyond the שבת limits.

phrases.english: and one tears the chicken for him,
and one cuts the leeks for him,
and one feeds him,
and one need not tithe; these are the words of Rabbi.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the ברייתא promised by the 'לימא תנאי היא' proposal.
steps.raayaObject: That רבה's ruling is disputed among תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the snake bite: רבי says no need to tithe.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון: he must not eat until it is tithed
steps.stepSummary: The other side of the ברייתא requires tithing before the sick person eats. This seems to match רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון says: he should not eat until one tithes.
steps.whatsHappening: The second opinion in the ברייתא is that the leeks must be tithed before he eats them. This completes the proposed dispute between תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון sounds like רבה (tithe first), while רבי sounds like he disagrees. The גמרא has framed this as a suggestion, so it may still be challenged.
steps.whatToRemember: The proposal: רבי (no need to tithe) seems to disagree with רבה, and רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון (tithe first) seems to agree with רבה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, says:
He should not eat until it is tithed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion in the same ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That רבה's ruling matches one side of a dispute between תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון's requirement to tithe before eating.

steps.title: Suggesting that רבה matches only רבי אלעזר son of רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws the conclusion of its proposed proof: רבה's rule seems to follow רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון and not רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that רבה's rule is the view of רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון, and not the view of רבי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the conclusion of the comparison it has been building. רבה seems to side with רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון, who requires tithing, and against רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, רבי said to feed the sick person without tithing. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון required tithing even though the produce was טבל only מדרבנן. Since רבה also requires tithing rabbinic טבל, he seems to agree with רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון. This would mean רבה's rule is disputed by a major תנא.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (introduces a suggestion the גמרא will test)

phrases.aramaic: נֵימָא רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הִיא,
phrases.english: Shall we say it is the view of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon,
phrases.notes: That is, רבה's rule follows him.

phrases.english: and not the view of Rabbi!
phrases.notes: רבי said to feed the sick person without tithing.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֵימָא רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the two sides of the ברייתא quoted in steps 7-8.
steps.raayaObject: That רבה's rule follows only one side of a dispute between תנאים
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about the snake-bitten person, where רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון requires tithing

steps.title: Even רבי agrees when the produce is grain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. רבי was lenient only about vegetable tithes, which are rabbinic. For grain, which is טבל by Torah law, even רבי requires tithing. Otherwise people might eat untithed grain from a perforated pot.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say רבה follows רבי. רבי was lenient there only about tithes from vegetables, which are a rabbinic law. But grain tithes are a Torah law. There, even רבי agrees that one must tithe. If you let a person eat grain from an עציץ שאינו נקוב without tithing, he will come to eat grain from an עציץ נקוב without tithing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last step. It shows that רבה's rule can fit רבי's view too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case in the ברייתא was vegetables, and tithing vegetables is only rabbinic. רבה's case is grain. Grain tithes are normally a Torah law, even though grain grown in an עציץ שאינו נקוב is only rabbinically טבל. Because it looks just like Torah-level טבל grain, even רבי would require tithing so that people do not get confused.

keyTerms.meaning: Even if you say (introduces a rejection: the rule can fit this view too)
Tithe from vegetables (only a rabbinic obligation)
A pot with a hole; produce grown in it counts as grown in the ground, so it is טבל מדאורייתא

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two 'rabbinic' cases. Vegetables are rabbinic as a whole category. Grain is a Torah category, and only this particular grain is rabbinic because of the pot it grew in. That difference is the whole answer.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבה's rule is no longer tied to one side of a dispute. Both תנאים can accept it, so it stands on firmer ground.

phrases.english: You can even say it follows Rabbi,

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי הָתָם —
phrases.english: Rabbi only said his ruling there
phrases.notes: Literally: 'until here רבי did not say there...'

phrases.english: regarding the vegetable tithe, which is rabbinic,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּמַעְשַׂר דָּגָן דְּטֶבֶל דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא הוּא,
phrases.english: but with the grain tithe, where untithed produce is a Torah-level category,
even Rabbi agrees that one must tithe,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי שָׁרֵית לֵיהּ בְּעָצִיץ שֶׁאֵינוֹ נָקוּב —
phrases.english: because if you permit it to him for grain from a pot without a hole,
he will come to eat grain from a pot with a hole, which is Torah-level untithed produce.
phrases.notes: This rule is there so people don't get confused.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא רַבִּי, עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 9's claim that רבה disagrees with רבי.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof is rejected as a whole. The ברייתא's dispute does not apply to רבה's case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא dealt with vegetables, which are rabbinic as a category. רבה dealt with grain, which is a Torah category, so even רבי would require tithing there.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה's rule (tithe first, even rabbinic טבל) fits both רבי and רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון, because grain looks like Torah-level טבל and could cause confusion.

steps.title: A person seized by בולמוס is fed honey and sweets
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא teaches that someone seized by בולמוס is fed honey and sweet foods, because they restore a person's eyesight. A verse about יונתן is brought as a hint, not as a proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: if someone is seized by בולמוס, we feed him honey and all kinds of sweet foods, because honey and sweets brighten a person's eyes. There is no full proof for this, but there is a hint: 'See how my eyes have brightened, because I tasted a little of this honey.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא about treating בולמוס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בולמוס is a dangerous attack of hunger that makes a person's vision go dark. The ברייתא gives the treatment, honey and sweets, and the reason: they restore eyesight. The verse is from שמואל א' (14:29), where יונתן ate honey and his eyes brightened. The ברייתא calls it only a 'hint' (זכר), which sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: A dangerous attack of extreme hunger that dims a person's eyesight
Brighten the light of his eyes (restore his vision)
A hint or allusion to the idea (weaker than a proof)

phrases.english: The Sages taught: one who is seized by bulmos,

phrases.aramaic: מַאֲכִילִין אוֹתוֹ דְּבַשׁ וְכׇל מִינֵי מְתִיקָה,
phrases.english: we feed him honey and all kinds of sweet foods,
because honey and all kinds of sweet foods
brighten the light of a person's eyes.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לַדָּבָר,
phrases.english: And although there is no proof for the matter,
there is a hint to the matter:
'See, please, how my eyes have brightened
phrases.notes: יונתן's words, שמואל א' 14:29

phrases.english: because I tasted a little of this honey.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: feeding a person seized by בולמוס.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person seized by בולמוס is fed honey and sweets, which restore eyesight. The verse about יונתן is only a hint.

steps.title: Why is the verse only a hint and not a proof?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא says there is 'no proof', when the verse about יונתן seems to prove the point directly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why does the ברייתא say 'although there is no proof for the matter'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's wording. The verse looks like a clear proof, so why call it just a hint?
steps.deeperAnalysis: יונתן said outright that honey brightened his eyes. That seems to be exactly what the ברייתא claims. So the phrase 'no proof' seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is meant by...? (questioning a phrase)

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי: ״אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לַדָּבָר״!
phrases.english: And why does it say: 'although there is no proof for the matter'?
phrases.notes: The verse seems to be a strong proof.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לַדָּבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the ברייתא in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's phrase 'אף על פי שאין ראיה לדבר'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse states directly that honey brightened יונתן's eyes, so it seems to be a full proof, not just a hint.

steps.title: יונתן was hungry, not seized by בולמוס
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: יונתן was not seized by בולמוס, only hungry. So the verse cannot prove what helps בולמוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because there, יונתן was not seized by בולמוס.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The verse is about ordinary hunger, not בולמוס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Honey helped יונתן's tired eyes, but he only had regular hunger. The ברייתא is talking about the dangerous condition of בולמוס. So the verse shows a similar effect, which makes it a fitting hint, but not a proof for this case.
steps.whatToRemember: Honey and sweets are the remedy for בולמוס. The verse about יונתן is only a 'hint' because he was just hungry, not seized by בולמוס.

phrases.english: Because there, bulmos had not seized him.
phrases.notes: יונתן was only very hungry.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the verse is about a different situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse about יונתן proves that honey cures בולמוס.
steps.terutzMaskana: יונתן was only hungry, not seized by בולמוס, so the verse is only a hint.

steps.title: אביי limits the honey rule: only after eating
steps.stepSummary: אביי says honey restores the eyes only after a person has eaten real food. Before eating, sweet food only makes the hunger stronger.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The ברייתא taught this only for after eating. Before eating, honey just stirs up the appetite.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי adds a limit to the ברייתא from step 11, which said honey and sweet foods restore the eyes of someone struck by בולמוס. He says this is true only after the person has already eaten some real food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא sounded like a general rule. אביי narrows it. On an empty stomach, sweets do not heal. They 'drag', meaning they pull out and sharpen the hunger. So the right order is real food first, then sweets.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They only taught this for…'. A formula that limits an earlier teaching to a specific case.
It surely drags / stirs up (the appetite)

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not arguing with the ברייתא. He agrees honey helps. He is only telling us WHEN it helps: after food, not before.

phrases.english: Abaye said: They did not teach this,
except for after eating;
but before eating, it only stirs up the appetite,
phrases.notes: Literally 'it surely drags', meaning it draws out more hunger.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לֹא שָׁנוּ, אֶלָּא לְאַחַר אֲכִילָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא of step 11 after the verse about יונתן was set aside, and limits its rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Honey and sweets heal בולמוס only after real food has been eaten. Before food, they increase the hunger.

steps.title: Proof from the Egyptian man fed by David's men
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings a פסוק: the Egyptian man was given bread and water first, and only afterward figs and raisins. Then his spirit returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'They found an Egyptian man in the field and brought him to דוד. They gave him bread and he ate, and they gave him water to drink. They gave him a piece of fig cake and two clusters of raisins, and he ate, and his spirit returned to him, because he had not eaten bread or drunk water for three days and three nights.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי proves his rule from a פסוק in שמואל. The starving Egyptian was given bread and water first, and only then sweet fruit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Look at the order in the פסוק: bread, then water, then fig cake and raisins. Only after the sweets does it say 'his spirit returned to him.' This shows that sweets heal when they come after real food, which is exactly אביי's point.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (introduces a verse as proof)
A piece of pressed fig cake
And his spirit returned to him

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And they found an Egyptian man in the field,
and they took him to David,
and they gave him bread and he ate,
and they gave him water to drink.
phrases.notes: First real food and drink.

phrases.aramaic: וַיִּתְּנוּ לוֹ פֶלַח דְּבֵילָה וּשְׁנֵי צִמּוּקִים
phrases.english: And they gave him a piece of fig cake and two clusters of raisins,
phrases.notes: Only now do the sweets come.

phrases.english: and he ate, and his spirit returned to him,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לֹא אָכַל לֶחֶם וְלֹא שָׁתָה מַיִם
phrases.english: for he had not eaten bread nor drunk water
for three days and three nights.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the scriptural support for אביי's limit.
steps.raayaObject: אביי's rule that sweets heal only after real food
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל א ל:יא-יב, the order of feeding the Egyptian man: bread and water first, then fig cake and raisins

steps.title: שמואל: feed him sheep's tail with honey
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן in the name of שמואל: someone struck by בולמוס is fed fatty sheep's tail with honey.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: Someone seized by בולמוס is fed a sheep's tail with honey.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a list of foods that cure בולמוס. The first one, from שמואל, is fatty sheep's tail eaten together with honey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This matches אביי's idea. Honey is paired with a solid, filling food instead of being given alone. The fat together with the sweetness strongly revives the person.

keyTerms.meaning: The fatty tail of a sheep

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said in the name of Shmuel:
One who is seized by bulmos,
we feed him sheep's tail with honey.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: מִי שֶׁאֲחָזוֹ בּוּלְמוּס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the general rule about sweets to specific remedies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person with בולמוס is fed sheep's tail with honey.

steps.title: רב הונא: fine wheat flour with honey also works
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע adds that fine wheat flour with honey is also a cure.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא the son of רב יהושע said: Also fine, clean flour with honey.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא adds another food to the list: fine wheat flour mixed with honey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אף' (also) shows he is adding to שמואל, not disagreeing. Honey can also be paired with fine wheat flour instead of sheep's tail.

keyTerms.meaning: Also / even (adds to the previous statement)

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said:
Also fine, clean flour with honey.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אָמַר: אַף סוֹלֶת נְקִיָּה בִּדְבַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the list of remedies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fine wheat flour with honey also cures בולמוס.

steps.title: רב פפא: even barley flour with honey works
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says that even cheap barley flour with honey is a cure.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Even barley flour with honey.
steps.whatsHappening: A third אמורא widens the list further: even simple barley flour with honey helps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each opinion goes one step lower in cost: sheep's tail, then fine wheat flour, then barley flour. 'אפילו' (even) shows this is the most extreme, cheapest option, so almost anyone can get the cure.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Even barley flour with honey.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ קִמְחָא דִשְׂעָרֵי בְּדוּבְשָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the list to the cheapest food.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even barley flour with honey cures בולמוס.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן ran to the east side of a fig tree
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן tells that when he was seized by בולמוס, he ran to the east side of a fig tree. He says his wisdom kept him alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Once I was seized by בולמוס, and I ran to the east side of a fig tree. I fulfilled in myself the verse: 'Wisdom keeps alive those who have it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן tells a personal story about how he saved himself from בולמוס with figs. He knew which side of the tree to go to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Figs do not all ripen at once. The ones facing the rising sun in the east ripen first and are sweetest. Because רבי יוחנן knew this, he found ripe figs quickly, so his knowledge literally saved his life.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Wisdom keeps alive those who have it' (קהלת ז:יב)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Once I was seized by bulmos,
and I ran to the east side of a fig tree,
phrases.notes: The east side ripens first, so the figs there were ready to eat.

phrases.english: and I fulfilled in myself:
'Wisdom keeps alive those who have it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: פַּעַם אַחַת אֲחָזַנִי בּוּלְמוּס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a real-life case of a sweet-food remedy (figs).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Ripe figs, found on the east side of the tree, helped cure רבי יוחנן's בולמוס.

steps.title: רב יוסף's teaching: the sun ripens figs from the east
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף's ברייתא explains רבי יוחנן's move: whoever wants the taste of a fig should turn to its east side, as the פסוק speaks of 'fruits of the sun.'
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יוסף taught: Whoever wants to taste the flavor of a fig should turn to its east side, as it says: 'And from the sweet things produced by the sun.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבי יוחנן ran to the east side. A teaching of רב יוסף says the east side of a fig tree has the tastiest figs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק connects good fruit with the sun. The morning sun shines first on the east side, so that fruit ripens and sweetens first. This is the 'wisdom' רבי יוחנן used.

keyTerms.meaning: The sweet produce of the sun (דברים לג:יד)

phrases.english: As Rav Yosef taught:
One who wants to taste the flavor of a fig
should turn to its east side,
as it is stated: 'And from the sweet things of the sun's produce.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתָנֵי רַב יוֹסֵף: הָרוֹצֶה לִטְעוֹם טַעַם תְּאֵנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the knowledge behind רבי יוחנן's story.
steps.raayaObject: Why רבי יוחנן went to the east side of the fig tree
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יוסף's ברייתא and דברים לג:יד, 'תבואות שמש'

steps.title: רבי יהודה takes a shepherd's bread
steps.stepSummary: While traveling, רבי יהודה was seized by בולמוס and grabbed a shepherd's bread. רבי יוסי told him, 'You robbed the shepherd.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי were walking on the road. רבי יהודה was seized by בולמוס. He overpowered a shepherd and ate his bread. רבי יוסי said to him: You robbed the shepherd.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story about two תנאים on a trip. This first half sets up a joke that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because בולמוס is life-threatening, רבי יהודה was allowed to take the bread to save his life. רבי יוסי playfully points out that he still took someone else's food. This line sets up רבי יהודה's comeback later.

keyTerms.meaning: They were walking on the road

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
were walking on the road.
Bulmos seized Rabbi Yehuda,
he overpowered a shepherd and ate his bread.
Rabbi Yosei said to him:
You robbed the shepherd.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הֲווֹ קָא אָזְלִי בְּאוֹרְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from remedies to stories of חכמים who suffered בולמוס.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person in danger from בולמוס may take food even from someone else.

steps.title: רבי יוסי 'robs' the whole city
steps.stepSummary: In the city, רבי יוסי was seized by בולמוס and the whole town brought him jugs and plates of food. רבי יהודה jokes: 'I robbed one shepherd, you robbed the whole city.'
steps.simpleTranslation: When they reached the city, רבי יוסי was seized by בולמוס. People surrounded him with jugs and plates. רבי יהודה said to him: I robbed the shepherd, and you robbed the entire city.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with a twist. Now רבי יוסי is the one struck by בולמוס, and רבי יהודה turns his words back on him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Out of respect, the townspeople rushed to bring רבי יוסי all kinds of food. רבי יהודה lightly teases him: if taking from one shepherd is 'robbing', then he took from a whole city. It is friendly humor, not a real accusation.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה is joking in a friendly way. He is not really saying רבי יוסי did something wrong.
steps.whatToRemember: בולמוס is treated as real danger. A person may eat whatever is needed, even someone else's food, and the חכמים themselves needed this help.

phrases.english: When they arrived at the town,
bulmos seized Rabbi Yosei.
They surrounded him with jugs and plates,
Rabbi Yehuda said to him:
I robbed the shepherd,
and you robbed the entire city.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי מְטוֹ לְמָתָא, אַחְזֵיה בּוּלְמוּס לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the story with the reversal and punchline.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Story conclusion: both חכמים needed food to survive בולמוס, with a friendly jab.

steps.title: New story: רבי מאיר paid attention to names
steps.stepSummary: With 'ותו' (and furthermore), the גמרא starts another travel story. רבי מאיר used to read meaning into people's names, but רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore: רבי מאיר, רבי יהודה, and רבי יוסי were walking on the road. רבי מאיר used to pay close attention to names. רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי did not pay attention to names.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new story with the same travelers plus רבי מאיר. It first tells us one key fact: רבי מאיר judged people by their names.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This background detail is the key to the whole story that follows. The story will test whether a name can show what kind of person someone is.

keyTerms.meaning: Paid close attention to names (read meaning into them)

phrases.english: And furthermore:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
were walking on the road.
Rabbi Meir would pay close attention to names;
Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
did not pay attention to names.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתוּ: רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הֲווֹ קָא אָזְלִי בְּאוֹרְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another story about the same חכמים traveling together.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Background: רבי מאיר read character from names, and the others did not.

steps.title: The innkeeper named כידור
steps.stepSummary: The travelers took lodging and asked the host's name. It was 'כידור', and רבי מאיר concluded he might be wicked, based on the פסוק 'כי דור תהפוכות המה.'
steps.simpleTranslation: When they came to a certain place, they asked for lodging and were given it. They asked him: What is your name? He said: 'כידור.' רבי מאיר said: Learn from this that he is a wicked man, as it says: 'For they are a generation (כי דור) of upheavals.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves forward: the host's name is כידור. רבי מאיר links it to a פסוק about a crooked generation and becomes suspicious of him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name כידור sounds exactly like 'כי דור' in דברים לב:כ, which describes a twisted, untrustworthy generation. רבי מאיר uses his name-reading method and decides this host cannot be trusted.

phrases.english: When they reached a certain place,
they sought lodging, and they were given it.
They said to him (the host): What is your name?
He said to them: 'Kidor.'

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ אָדָם רָשָׁע הוּא,
phrases.english: He (Rabbi Meir) said: Learn from this that he is a wicked man,
as it is stated: 'For they are a generation of upheavals.'

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי מְטוֹ לְהָהוּא דּוּכְתָּא, בְּעוֹ אוּשְׁפִּיזָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבי מאיר's name-reading habit to the host.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר suspects the host is wicked because his name echoes 'כי דור תהפוכות.'

steps.title: Who trusted the innkeeper with their money
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי left their purses with the host. רבי מאיר did not, and instead hid his purse at the grave of the host's father.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי handed over their purses to him. רבי מאיר did not hand over his purse to him. He went and placed it at the grave of the host's father.
steps.whatsHappening: The story shows how each rabbi acted on his view. The two who ignored names trusted the host, while רבי מאיר hid his money elsewhere. The outcome comes in steps 26-33.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because of the approaching שבת, travelers would leave their money with someone for safekeeping. רבי מאיר acted on his suspicion and put his purse in a separate place, at the father's grave. The next steps (26-33) tell how the story ends.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
entrusted their purses to him.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר לָא אַשְׁלֵים לֵיהּ כִּיסֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir did not entrust his purse to him;
he went and placed it at the grave of his (the host's) father.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אַשְׁלִימוּ לֵיהּ כִּיסַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the practical result of each rabbi's attitude toward names.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר acted on his suspicion and did not trust the host, while the others did. The story continues next.

steps.title: The innkeeper's dream about the hidden purse
steps.stepSummary: The innkeeper's dead father appears to him in a dream and tells him to take the purse lying at 'that man's' head. The innkeeper tells the חכמים about the dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: It appeared to him in his dream: 'Come, take the purse placed at the head of that man.' The next day he said to them: 'This is what appeared to me in my dream.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. The purse רבי מאיר hid at the father's grave is revealed in a dream to the innkeeper, who tells the Sages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'That man' is a polite way of saying the father himself, so the dream points straight to the grave where רבי מאיר hid his purse. Now רבי מאיר's hiding place is in danger.

phrases.english: It appeared to him in his dream:
phrases.notes: The innkeeper's dead father appeared to the innkeeper.

phrases.english: Come, take the purse
that is placed at the head of that man.
phrases.notes: 'That man' means the father himself, a polite way of not saying 'me'.

phrases.english: The next day he said to them:
This is what appeared to me in my dream.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows directly from רבי מאיר hiding his purse at the father's grave.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The hidden purse is revealed to the innkeeper in a dream.

steps.title: The חכמים dismiss the dream, but רבי מאיר moves his purse
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say dreams at twilight on Friday night mean nothing. רבי מאיר still guards his purse all day and then takes it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'Dreams of twilight have no substance.' רבי מאיר went, guarded it all day, and brought it back.
steps.whatsHappening: The Sages brush the dream off. רבי מאיר does not rely on that and quietly rescues his money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dream came at twilight on ערב שבת, so the Sages treat it as meaningless. רבי מאיר could not carry the purse on שבת, so he watched over it all day and took it once he could. His caution fits his habit of being suspicious based on names.

phrases.english: They said to him:

phrases.aramaic: חֶלְמָא דְּבֵי שִׁמְשֵׁי לֵית בְּהוּ מַמָּשָׁא,
phrases.english: Dreams of twilight have no substance,
phrases.notes: Twilight of ערב שבת.

phrases.aramaic: אֲזַל רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְנַטְרֵיהּ כּוּלֵּי יוֹמָא
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir went and guarded it all day
and brought it.
phrases.notes: He took it after שבת.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֶלְמָא דְּבֵי שִׁמְשֵׁי לֵית בְּהוּ מַמָּשָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The response to the dream reported in Step 26.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Twilight dreams are dismissed, yet רבי מאיר acts with caution and saves his purse.

steps.title: The innkeeper denies ever receiving the purses
steps.stepSummary: After שבת, רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי ask for their purses. The innkeeper claims it never happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: The next day they said to him: 'Give us our purses.' He said to them: 'These things never happened.'
steps.whatsHappening: The danger רבי מאיר suspected comes true. The innkeeper steals the other Sages' money by denying they ever gave it to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows that רבי מאיר's reading of the name כידור (from 'דור תהפוכות') was correct. The two Sages who trusted the host lose their money, at least for now.

keyTerms.meaning: these things never happened (a flat denial)

phrases.english: The next day they said to him:
Give us our purses.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: לֹא הָיוּ דְבָרִים מֵעוֹלָם.
phrases.english: He said to them: These things never happened.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The result of רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי trusting the host in Step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The host denies the deposit, which proves he was wicked as his name hinted.

steps.title: רבי מאיר asks why they ignored the name
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר asks his colleagues why they did not look into the host's name.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר said to them: 'Why didn't you examine his name?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר gently scolds his colleagues for not paying attention to the name כידור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects back to Step 23, where רבי מאיר paid attention to names and the others did not. His question is really a reproach, not a request for information.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir said to them:
Why didn't you examine the name?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to the loss described in Step 28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Paying attention to a name could have warned them.

steps.title: The חכמים ask why רבי מאיר did not warn them
steps.stepSummary: The other חכמים answer back: if you suspected him, why didn't you tell us?
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'Why didn't the Master tell us?'
steps.whatsHappening: The colleagues turn the question around and ask why רבי מאיר kept his suspicion to himself. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their point is that if רבי מאיר thought the host was dangerous, he should have warned them too. The question pushes רבי מאיר to explain how strong his suspicion really was.

phrases.english: They said to him:
Why didn't the Master tell us?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי מאיר's question in Step 29 with a question of their own.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי מאיר did not share his suspicion about the host.

steps.title: A name is a reason for caution, not proof
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר explains that a name only calls for caution. It is not enough to label a person as wicked.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'I said one should be suspicious. Did I say one should treat him as definitely wicked?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר answers that the name only made him careful himself. He could not accuse the host to others based on a name alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two levels here: חשש (being careful) and חזקה (treating something as established fact). A name allows you to protect yourself quietly. It does not allow you to brand a person as wicked.

keyTerms.meaning: to establish as a fact (treat as definitely so)

steps.whyThisMatters: It draws a clear line between being careful for yourself and accusing someone else. That line is a useful lesson about suspecting people.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Granted, I said to be suspicious,
but did I say to establish him as wicked?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A name allows personal caution (חשש) but not treating someone as established wicked (חזקה).

steps.title: The lentil sign recovers the purses
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים take the innkeeper to a tavern and see lentils on his mustache. They give that 'sign' to his wife and collect their purses.
steps.simpleTranslation: They dragged him and brought him into a shop. They saw lentils on his mustache. They went and gave this sign to his wife, took their purses, and brought them back.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים use a clever trick to get their money back from the innkeeper's wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They pretended the husband had sent them, and they 'proved' it with a private detail: he had just eaten lentils. The wife believed them and handed over the purses. The trick only worked because he had not washed his mouth after eating.

phrases.english: They dragged him and brought him into a shop,
phrases.notes: They gave him wine to drink.

phrases.english: they saw lentils on his mustache,
they went and gave the sign to his wife
phrases.notes: They claimed the husband said to return the money on this sign.

phrases.english: and they took their purses and brought them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the loss from Step 28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Sages recover their purses using the lentil sign.

steps.title: The innkeeper kills his wife
steps.stepSummary: Furious that his wife gave back the money, the innkeeper kills her.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and killed his wife.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends tragically: the wicked host murders his wife out of anger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows how wicked כידור really was. It also sets up the closing ברייתא, which ties the death to his failure to wash after eating.

phrases.english: He went and killed his wife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The result of the wife returning the purses in Step 32.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The innkeeper kills his wife.

steps.title: The lesson of first and last hand-washing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא links the story to a ברייתא. Skipping the first washing led to someone being fed pork, and skipping the final washing led to a death.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what we learned: 'The first waters caused someone to be fed pork. The last waters killed a person.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the story by connecting it to a known teaching about מים ראשונים and מים אחרונים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'First waters' refers to a different story. An innkeeper served pork to anyone who did not wash before eating, assuming he was not Jewish. 'Last waters' fits our story: had כידור washed after eating, the lentils would not have been on his mustache, and his wife would not have been killed.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר's caution based on a name saved his money. A name is a reason for caution (חשש), not proof (חזקה). Not washing after a meal (מים אחרונים) led to a death in this story.
steps.confusionAlert: 'The last waters killed a person' does not mean the water itself killed anyone. It means that skipping the after-meal washing left the lentils visible, and that chain of events ended in the wife's death.

phrases.english: This is what we learned:
The first waters caused someone to be fed pork.
phrases.notes: Lack of washing before the meal.

phrases.english: The last waters killed a person.
phrases.notes: Lack of washing after the meal, as in our story.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects the whole כידור story to a ברייתא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Neglecting מים אחרונים led to a death; the story shows this teaching in action.

steps.title: The חכמים also start paying attention to names
steps.stepSummary: In the end, רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי also judged people by their names. They refused to stay at the house of a man named בלה and concluded that he was wicked.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, they too would pay attention to names. When they came to a house whose owner was named 'בלה', they did not go in to him. They said: we can learn from this that he is wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the lesson learned. רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי now act like רבי מאיר and are careful about a person's name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the two Sages did not pay attention to names and lost their money. Now they have changed their approach. When they meet a man named בלה, they stay away from him and conclude that he is wicked.

keyTerms.meaning: They paid close attention to names
A man's name; it sounds like 'worn out'
Learn from this / we can conclude

steps.whatToRemember: The story ends with the חכמים agreeing with רבי מאיר that a person's name can be a warning sign.

phrases.english: And in the end, they too would pay attention to names.
When they came to a certain house
whose owner was named 'Bala',
they did not go in to him.
They said: Conclude from this that he is wicked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the final outcome of the innkeeper story. The Sages now take on רבי מאיר's habit.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי came to pay attention to names. A name like בלה warned them that the man was wicked.

steps.title: A verse shows why the name בלה suggests wickedness
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים bring a פסוק in יחזקאל that uses the word בלה for someone worn out by immorality. A פסוק in בראשית shows that the word means 'grown old'.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And I said of her who was בלה with adulteries.' The word is like 'After I have grown old [בלותי], shall I have pleasure?' That means: she grew old in adulteries.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for why the name בלה is a bad sign. It quotes a פסוק where בלה describes someone worn out by sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word בלה comes from the root meaning 'worn out' or 'old', as in שרה's words 'אחרי בלותי'. In יחזקאל, 'לבלה נאופים' describes someone who grew old through adulteries. So the name hints at a wicked person.

keyTerms.meaning: My growing old / being worn out

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And I said of her who was worn out by adulteries' (Ezekiel 23:43),
(like the verse: 'After I have grown old, shall I have pleasure?' (Genesis 18:12),
that is to say: she grew old in adulteries).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the Sages' conclusion in step 35 with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That the name בלה hints that its owner is wicked.
steps.raayaSupportSource: יחזקאל כג:מג ('לבלה נאופים'), explained through בראשית יח:יב ('אחרי בלותי').

steps.title: Five signs of a mad dog
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about someone bitten by a כלב שוטה. It brings a ברייתא listing five signs that show a dog is mad.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One whom a mad dog bit, etc.' The Rabbis taught: Five things were said about a mad dog. Its mouth is open, its saliva drips, its ears hang down, its tail rests on its legs, and it walks along the sides of roads.
steps.whatsHappening: The אגדה is over. The גמרא now returns to the משנה and explains how to recognize a כלב שוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה spoke about someone bitten by a mad dog, so we need to know what counts as a mad dog. The ברייתא gives five physical and behavioral signs for identifying one.
steps.confusionAlert: The words 'מי שנשכו כלב שוטה וכו׳' are not a new statement. They quote the משנה to show which topic the גמרא is now explaining.

phrases.english: [The Mishnah stated:] One whom a mad dog bit, etc.
The Rabbis taught:
Five signs were said about a mad dog:
its mouth is open, and its saliva drips,
and its ears hang down,
and its tail rests on its legs,
and it walks along the sides of roads.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי שֶׁנְּשָׁכוֹ כֶּלֶב שׁוֹטֶה וְכוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story and returns to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כלב שוטה is recognized by five signs: open mouth, dripping saliva, hanging ears, tail resting on its legs, and walking at the sides of roads.

steps.title: Some add a sixth sign: a silent bark
steps.stepSummary: A second opinion in the ברייתא adds another sign. The dog barks, but its voice is not heard.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: it also barks, but its voice is not heard.
steps.whatsHappening: Another view in the same ברייתא adds one more sign to the list of five.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The יש אומרים does not argue with the five signs. It adds a sixth: the dog seems to bark, but no sound comes out.

phrases.english: And some say:
it also barks, but its voice is not heard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds one more sign to the five signs in step 37.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the יש אומרים, a silent bark is also a sign of a mad dog.

steps.title: What makes a dog go mad?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what causes a dog to become mad.
steps.simpleTranslation: From what does it come about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question about the cause of the dog's madness. This sets up the next step, where רב and שמואל answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We now know how to recognize a mad dog. The גמרא wants to know what causes the condition. This is a request for information, not a challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: From what does it come about? / What causes it?

phrases.english: From what does it [the madness] come about?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the signs of the mad dog to the cause of its madness.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What causes a dog to become a כלב שוטה.

steps.title: רב and שמואל: witchcraft or an evil spirit
steps.stepSummary: רב says witches play with the dog through their sorcery. שמואל says an evil spirit rests on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Witches are playing with it. And שמואל said: An evil spirit rests on it.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים give different answers to the question of what makes a dog mad.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב says the cause comes from people: witches use magic on the dog. שמואל says the cause is a רוח רעה that settles on the dog. Both say the cause is outside the dog, but they disagree about what it is.

keyTerms.meaning: Play with it (use magic on it)

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: נָשִׁים כַּשְׁפָנִיּוֹת מְשַׂחֲקוֹת בּוֹ,
phrases.english: Rav said: Witches are playing with it [through sorcery],

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: רוּחַ רָעָה שׁוֹרָה עָלָיו.
phrases.english: and Shmuel said: An evil spirit rests upon it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: נָשִׁים כַּשְׁפָנִיּוֹת מְשַׂחֲקוֹת בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 39 with two opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב: witchcraft causes the madness. שמואל: an evil spirit causes it.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between them?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the views of רב and שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the disagreement between רב and שמואל changes anything in practice. This sets up the answer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree on the signs of a mad dog, so the argument might seem to be only about theory. The גמרא wants to find a concrete case where the two views lead to different results.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the (practical) difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the practical difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the practical result of the disagreement in step 40.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical difference that results from רב's view versus שמואל's view.

steps.title: There is a practical difference
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to answer: there is indeed a practical difference between them. The details continue on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them...
steps.whatsHappening: This is the opening of the answer. The גמרא is setting up its explanation, which continues past the end of this passage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase איכא בינייהו tells us the argument does have a real effect. What that effect is will be explained right after this line.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a (practical) difference between them

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is cut off here. The actual difference is stated on the next amud, so do not look for it in this line.

phrases.english: There is a practical difference between them with regard to...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 41.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: There is a practical difference. The details follow on the next amud.
